source.snippet: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers. Comment: 'In their defense, the $50 fares aren't profitable on its own. It costs $140 to fly this two-seater plane... Charging one of them $100 (that their company would pay for anyway) makes it possible for both to fly.' — Discussion thread on airlines actively blocking AI booking agents, surfacing a gap between enterprise travel automation and airline policy enforcement.

problem_statement: Enterprises and business travelers using AI agents for travel booking face active blocking by airlines, leaving corporate travel managers without a compliant automated booking workflow and forcing manual fallbacks.
target_segment: Corporate travel managers and finance ops teams at mid-to-large companies spending on managed travel programs.
notes: Company travel budgets are explicit (commenter notes company paying $100 fares). Airlines blocking AI agents creates a compliance and workflow gap — opportunity for a middleware or policy-aware travel agent layer that remains compliant while automating booking. Buyer is the corporate travel manager or CFO-adjacent ops role with real budget.
